In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

udf: check the unallocated space table when it is loaded

udf_table_new_block() hands out the first block of the extent closest
to its goal and trusts that the extent covers at least one whole block
inside the partition.  Nothing checks that.  A zero-length extent makes
it return the block the extent points at, which need not be free, and
the subtraction of one block then underflows the length into the type
bits, turning the entry into a bogus continuation.  An extent running
past the end of the partition makes it return blocks behind the
partition.

Such tables are not only found on crafted images: until the previous
commit, udf_table_new_block() itself left zero-length extents behind
in tables written by mkudffs, and then converted them into extents
running past the partition.

Check every extent once when the table is loaded, and refuse
read-write access if one is empty, is not a whole number of blocks, or
does not lie inside the partition, in the same way as for other
allocation information the kernel cannot use.  Check first that the
table is an Unallocated Space Entry at all: the walk starts at the
offset of the allocation descriptors in one, and for a file entry that
offset lies before the inode's in-memory copy of the descriptors.
Treat a chain of allocation extent descriptors that leads back to
itself the same way: the walk would otherwise return the same extents
forever, and the mount would never finish.  Let a fatal signal
interrupt the walk and fail the mount.

Refusing read-write access to an empty extent is deliberate.  It shows
that an old kernel took the last block but left the entry behind.  If
consumed again, the entry returns an in-use block and turns into a huge
bogus extent.  Refusing the table before that
happens avoids this second allocation; the filesystem can still be
mounted read-only.  The check cannot detect every overlap that may
already exist in a damaged table.

This patch should be backported together with the previous one: that
patch stops creating new empty extents, and this one rejects existing
ones before they are consumed again.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mptcp: pm: kernel: use RCU to free endpoint listeners

mptcp_pm_nl_create_listen_socket() starts the TCP listener directly
instead of going through mptcp_listen(). It consequently misses setting
SOCK_RCU_FREE on the parent MPTCP socket.

tcp_child_process() can invoke the listener's subflow_data_ready()
callback without holding the MPTCP parent lock or a reference to the
parent. An authenticated MP_JOIN racing with endpoint teardown can
therefore access the parent after its last reference has been dropped.
The ADD_ADDR error path can also close an already published listener.

Set SOCK_RCU_FREE before __inet_listen_sk() publishes the TCP listener,
matching mptcp_listen(). This protects the parent on every subsequent
close path, including a failed endpoint addition.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: usx2y: Require a buffer of two URBs

usx2y_urb_capt_retire() wraps the ring buffer once per packet and
usx2y_urb_play_prepare() once per URB of nr_of_packs() packets of up to
50 frames. Both assume that the data fits in the buffer, and the hw
constraints only require about two 1 ms periods, so a packet larger
than the buffer on capture, or a URB larger than the buffer on playback,
violates that assumption.

Constrain SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_SIZE in snd_usx2y_pcm_open() to at
least two URBs, 2 * nr_of_packs() * 50 frames, for both directions. The
bound is in frames and derived from the driver's own packet limit, so it
does not read the endpoint, whose altsetting is only selected in
prepare. Two URBs rather than one, because the position advances by a
URB on playback and only moves when a URB is less than the whole buffer.
Keep a guard in usx2y_urb_capt_retire() that drops a packet larger than
the buffer, for the case the constraint makes unreachable.

With nrpacks above about 163 (S16_LE) or 109 (S24_3LE) the bound exceeds
the 64 KiB buffer the substream preallocates (twice that with the
preallocation raised to its 128 KiB maximum), so hw_params fails for
those module settings. That is intended: the driver cannot be safe with
a URB larger than half the largest buffer.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the US-122
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 512-byte capture buffer:

  BUG: KASAN: out-of-bounds in i_usx2y_urb_complete+0x1285/0x1ac0
  Read of size 18446744073709551104 at addr ffff88800e448800 by task vhci_rx/83

Tested on 7.3-rc7 with the same device, S16_LE at 44100 Hz, nrpacks 4,
so the bound is 400 frames. A 128-frame capture buffer and a 200-frame
playback buffer are refused at hw_params with EINVAL. A 400-frame buffer
streams for 30 s in each direction with the position advancing inside
the buffer and no KASAN report; the capture guard did not fire. The
same 400-frame capture buffer with S24_3LE, which selects altsetting 2
in prepare, streams for 30 s with the same result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Reject capture buffers smaller than two packets

line6_capture_copy() splits the copy into the ALSA ring buffer once at
the buffer end and wraps pos_done once, which is only correct when one
packet holds at most buffer_size frames. The packet size comes from the
device's endpoint, and the per-device hw structs allow 64-byte periods
with periods_min 1, so a packet can be larger than the whole buffer.
audio_in_callback() logs an oversized packet and then copies it anyway.

The packet size is known at probe time, so constrain
SNDRV_PCM_HW_PARAM_BUFFER_BYTES in snd_line6_capture_open() to at least
twice the larger of the two endpoints' packet sizes. Two rather than
one, because pos_done advances by the packet and wraps once, so a buffer
of exactly one packet leaves the position unchanged after every packet.
hw_params then rejects a buffer that cannot hold two packets, and the
single wrap is valid for every configuration that gets through. Keep a
guard in line6_capture_copy() that drops an oversized packet with a
ratelimited error, for the case that should no longer be reachable.

Reproduced on 7.3-rc7 with a USB/IP device presenting the GuitarPort
interface layout and 1024-byte packets into a 128-byte buffer: ALSA
logged "invalid position: pos = 224, buffer size = 32" and the driver
logged "driver bug: len" on every following packet. With this patch a
1024-byte buffer is refused at hw_params, and a 2048-byte buffer streams
for 30 s with no report and with the position moving inside the buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/ksm: fix use of a freed anon_vma at swap-in

A folio read from a swap slot previously shared by KSM can remain in the
swap cache after the process that first mapped it exits. Its anon_vma
can then be freed, so ksm_might_need_to_copy() must not dereference it
to compare roots.

Doing so can result in some false-positives, resulting in the reverse
mapping missing the new folio mapping, preventing migration and reclaim.

SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU allows individual anon_vma objects to be reused
immediately after freeing. A stale pointer can then refer to another
anon_vma whose root matches, even though the target VMA is not linked
to that anon_vma.

Move the anonymous rmap compatibility checks into
folio_anon_rmap_compatible(). Keep the page-index check and compare the
folio's anon_vma pointer against the VMA's own anon_vma and root first.

If neither matches, bite the bullet and walk the VMA's anon_vma_chain.
The VMA keeps these anon_vmas alive, and finding a match guarantees that
reverse mapping can find the new mapping.

Lorenzo Stoakes says in a private discussion:

  "This isn't quite equivalent to the existing check.

  Every anon_vma in an anon_vma_chain shares the same root, but if you
  split a VMA then fork both of them like this:

                  VMA A
               /        \         <split>
            VMA B      VMA C
               \        /
        root <- anon_vma 1
               ----^ ^----        <fork>
              /   parent  \
        anon_vma 2   anon_vma 3
             |            |
           VMA D        VMA E

  VMA's D and E both get their own new
  anon_vma's such that:

  VMA D: anon_vma 2 -> anon_vma 1 -> root
  VMA E: anon_vma 3 -> anon_vma 1 -> root

  And if you found a folio referencing anon_vma 2, the existing check:

	anon_vma->root == vma->anon-vma->root

  Would be true for VMA's B, C, D & E.

  However after your change it'd be true for VMA D only, as it's the only
  one with anon_vma 2 in its anon_vma_chain.

  Whether or not that could actually happen in practice... 🙂 I don't
  know.

  [...] after your change it'd be true for VMA D only, as it's the only
  one with anon_vma 2 in its anon_vma_chain. [...] I would [...] say that
  you are making the test stricter but more correct.
"

If this affects performance when KSM was never even involved, we could
just track whether KSM ever merged anything and just skip these checks.

There isn't really a lot we can do otherwise: for mapped folios we might
be able to use folio_get_anon_vma(), but for unmapped folios there really
is no easy way to see if the anon_vma is still valid.

Document the (confusing) lifetime requirements of folio_anon_vma().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock

The receive lists of a CAN device are located in the device's
can_ml_priv and travel with the device when it is moved to another
network namespace. But they are protected by the per-netns
rcvlists_lock. So can_rx_unregister() needs dev_net(dev) to pick the
right lock and silently returns when the passed namespace does not
match dev_net(dev) anymore.

isotp_release() and bcm_release() leave their notifier list before they
take any lock that serializes against the netdev notifier, which runs
under RTNL. When the bound device is moved to another namespace in this
window, the notifier skips the socket and the release path has to remove
the filters itself. isotp_release() passes the socket's namespace, which
does not match dev_net(dev) anymore. bcm_rx_unreg() passes dev_net(dev),
which can_rx_unregister() reads again for its check, so a namespace
change between both reads makes the check fail as well. In both cases
can_rx_unregister() silently returns. As can_rx_register() stores
rcv->sk without a reference, the remaining receivers point to the freed
socket (isotp) or the freed op (bcm):

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in isotp_rcv+0x1570/0x24d0
  Read of size 1 at addr ffff888118130552 by task isotp_ns_uaf/578
   can_rcv_filter+0x4af/0x8c0
   can_receive+0x28d/0x3c0
   can_rcv+0x2a9/0x310
   __netif_receive_skb_one_core+0x21a/0x260
   process_backlog+0x210/0x760

Besides this, the lists of a device are protected by the rcvlists_lock
of the namespace that is passed in. Callers which pass dev_net(dev) read
it at different times, so the same lists may be modified under the locks
of different namespaces while the device is moved.

Taking RTNL in these release paths is no option: raw_bind(),
raw_setsockopt() and raw_release() already hold RTNL while adding and
removing up to CAN_RAW_FILTER_MAX filters per socket, which unprivileged
users can trigger repeatedly and which makes RTNL a global bottleneck.

Instead fix the root cause and add a spinlock to struct
can_dev_rcv_lists, which protects the receive lists of a CAN device or
the 'any' CAN device lists of a namespace. It is initialized in
can_set_ml_priv(), which is used by all CAN network devices. With this,
can_rx_unregister() finds the subscription independently of the
current namespace of the device. The protocols keep the device valid
with their tracked references. The per-netns rcvlists_lock only protects
the receive list statistics anymore, and CAN_RAW, CAN_BCM and CAN_ISOTP
pass the namespace that has been used for can_rx_register().

So isotp_release() and bcm_release() now remove their filters correctly
without RTNL, and raw_release(), raw_setsockopt(), raw_bind() and
isotp_bind() do not need RTNL anymore and add and remove their filters
under lock_sock(). To serialize bind() with NETDEV_UNREGISTER, bind()
publishes the device inside the RCU section of its lookup, and
raw_notify() and isotp_notify() recheck the bound device under lock_sock().
As RTNL does not keep NETDEV_DOWN out of bind() anymore, bind() checks
IFF_UP after publishing the bound device, with a barrier pair against
raw_notify() and isotp_notify(), so a down transition during bind() is
still reported with ENETDOWN.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: dev: can_dropped_invalid_skb: drop CAN XL frames on non-CAN XL devices

Sending a PF_PACKET bypasses the CAN framework logic and can directly
reach a CAN driver's xmit() function. The PF_PACKET framework only
checks that skb->len does not exceed the net_device MTU.

For a CAN device that is not CAN XL capable, anything above CANFD_MTU
(72 bytes) is therefore dropped before it reaches the driver. However,
CAN XL frames are variable length. can_is_canxl_skb() accepts lengths in
the range CANXL_HDR_SIZE + CANXL_MIN_DLEN up to CANXL_MTU, i.e. 13 to
2060 bytes.

As a result, an ETH_P_CANXL skb with a length between 13 and 72 bytes
can pass both the MTU and the can_dropped_invalid_skb() checks.

A driver that does not support CAN XL will interpret canxl_frame->flags
as a length because of the overlap with can_frame->len. And because
CANXL_XLF is set, the resulting length is between 128 and 255. For
drivers that do not check can_frame->len before copying can_frame->data,
as most drivers do, this results in a buffer overflow of up to 247
bytes.

Drop ETH_P_CANXL skbs if the device does not have the CAN_CAP_XL
capability. Keep can_is_canxl_skb() for the validation of CAN XL skbs.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order

vhost_add_used_n_in_order() advances start by nheads[i] but wraps it
with a single subtraction.  If start + nheads[i] >= 2 * vq->num, start
can remain outside the ring.

With used-ring logging enabled, start > vq->num makes (vq->num - start)
underflow.  log_write() then sets bits beyond the dirty-log bitmap,
potentially corrupting adjacent userspace memory.  This is reachable on
the vhost-net TX path with VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER: done_idx can reach
VHOST_NET_BATCH (64), triggering the issue with a 32-entry ring.

Wrap start with a mask to keep it within the ring.  VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM
enforces a nonzero power-of-two ring size, allowing start to be wrapped
using & (vq->num - 1).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement

qfq_change_class() snapshots the current aggregate settings while
holding the qdisc tree lock, but drops the lock before selecting the
destination aggregate. During that gap, qfq_enqueue() can move the
class to an aggregate matching the requested settings.

When qfq_change_class() resumes, qfq_find_agg() then returns cl->agg.
If it is a singleton, qfq_deact_rm_from_agg() frees the aggregate
before qfq_add_to_agg() immediately accesses the same pointer, causing
a use-after-free.

While holding the tree lock, skip the replacement when the destination
is already the current aggregate. Any estimator replacement has already
completed, so the class change can finish normally.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks

ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock() drops the inode reference before releasing the
DENTRY lock.  This lets inode eviction release the local inode and open
locks before a remote unlink can proceed past the DENTRY lock.

A DLM callback can still arrive before the DENTRY lock has been dropped.
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb() obtains the mount context through dl_inode->i_sb,
which can access a freed inode when the downconvert thread drops the
last inode reference in its post-unlock callback:

  Downconvert thread                     DLM callback thread
  ------------------                     -------------------
  ocfs2_process_blocked_lock()
    ocfs2_dentry_post_unlock()
      ocfs2_dentry_lock_put()
        ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock()
          iput(dl->dl_inode)
          [inode reclaimed after RCU]
                                         ocfs2_blocking_ast()
                                           ocfs2_get_dentry_osb()
                                             dl->dl_inode->i_sb
          ocfs2_simple_drop_lockres()

Store the mount context in the DENTRY lock resource's l_priv field and use
the default mount-context lookup.  Recover the containing dentry lock with
container_of(), as already done for refcount locks, and remove
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb().  ocfs2_dismount_volume() shuts down the DLM before
freeing the mount context, so callbacks can use it without accessing the
inode.  Preserve the existing iput-before-unlock order to avoid delaying
local inode and open lock release until after the DENTRY lock is released.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: memcontrol: fix NULL pointer deref and UAF from high_work_func() on dying memcg

When memory.high is exceeded in non-task context, try_charge_memcg()
schedules memcg->high_work without taking a reference on the memcg, and
high_work_func() invokes reclaim_high() without pinning the memcg.

With obj_cgroup reparenting, introduced in commit bf4f059954dc ("mm:
memcg/slab: obj_cgroup API"), objects charged to a child memcg are
reparented to its parent in mem_cgroup_css_offline() instead of holding a
reference on the child until uncharged.  Subsequent uncharges of those
objects go to the parent, which can leave the child's memory use
permanently above its high limit, so any later charge on the offlined
memcg in non-task context schedules high_work.  This was later widened
from kernel memory to LRU folios when commit f1cf8d2f36dc ("mm:
memcontrol: eliminate the problem of dying memory cgroup for LRU folios")
converted LRU folios to use obj_cgroup reparenting.

cancel_work_sync(&memcg->high_work) only runs at the end of teardown in
mem_cgroup_css_free(), so high_work_func() can start or still be running
reclaim_high() after mem_cgroup_css_released() or shrink_many() has called
lru_gen_release_memcg() and unhashed lruvec->lrugen.list.  If reclaim
tries to rotate the memcg, lru_gen_rotate_memcg() dereferences a NULL
pprev pointer.  This issue is specific to MGLRU and was introduced with
the memcg LRU in commit e4dde56cd208 ("mm: multi-gen LRU: per-node
lru_gen_folio lists").

With either traditional LRU or MGLRU, css_free_rwork_fn() calls
css_rstat_exit() which frees per-CPU rstat data before calling
mem_cgroup_css_free().  If reclaim_high() is still running, rstat updates
via mod_lruvec_state() -> __css_rstat_updated() cause a use-after-free on
the per-CPU rstat data.  This was introduced when commit 5da3bfa029d6
("cgroup: use separate rstat trees for each subsystem") moved
css_rstat_exit() ahead of ss->css_free().

Fix both problems by acquiring a reference with css_tryget_online() in
high_work_func() before calling reclaim_high(), and by resetting
memory.high and swap.high to PAGE_COUNTER_MAX in mem_cgroup_css_offline()
so that charges via references on an offlined memcg do not trigger
high_work on the dead child and skip checking live ancestors in
try_charge_memcg().

Acquiring the reference in high_work_func() rather than before scheduling
high_work is safe because mem_cgroup_css_free() calls irq_work_sync() and
cancel_work_sync() which cancels pending work and waits for an already
running high_work_func() to complete before mem_cgroup_free() frees the
memcg.  css_tryget_online() uses percpu_ref_tryget_live() and is safe to
call after percpu_ref_exit() before the cgroup is freed unlike
css_tryget().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio

collapse_file() can fail its reference-count or dirty-folio check after
unmapping with TTU_BATCH_FLUSH.  Both paths put back the isolated folio,
then unlock it and drop the lookup reference before reaching the common
try_to_unmap_flush().

The page-cache reference does not keep the folio stable once the lock is
released.  Another collapse can replace and free it.  With its PTEs
already gone, that collapse cannot flush the first task's per-task TLB
batch, and retract_page_tables() skips short or unaligned VMAs.  A CPU can
therefore retain a user translation to the freed folio.  This has been
reproduced with unprivileged MADV_COLLAPSE on a memfd.

Flush at out_unlock while the lookup reference and folio lock are still
held.  The common flush continues to cover the accumulated pagelist on
both success and rollback, preserving batching on successful collapses.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ntfs: don't allow compression on volumes with clusters larger than 4K

On a volume made with "mkntfs -c 8192", a user can set
FILE_ATTR_COMPRESSED on an empty file through system.ntfs_attrib.
Writing to the file and reading it back after dropping the page cache
then crashes:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in ntfs_read_compressed_block+0xa2c/0x2040
  Read of size 8192 at addr ffff88804355a000 by task dd/106

The read path only handles clusters up to 4K. It copies each cluster
out of a single page, and a compression block of 16 8K clusters does
not fit in the 64K ntfs_compression_buffer. Loading an inode already
rejects compressed data on such volumes.

Reject the flag change the same way.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: fix list corruption when deferred_split_scan() races with deferred_split_folio()

Since the deferred split queue became a list_lru, the isolate callback
moves the folios it took a reference on to an on-stack list, linked
through folio->_deferred_list, and deferred_split_scan() takes them off
that list with list_del_init() without holding the list_lru lock.

deferred_split_folio() does not know about the on-stack list. It only
holds the list_lru lock when it looks at the same list_head, and it can
run for such a folio: a THP is queued when it is mapped, as a candidate
for the underused check, and is queued "again" when a part of it gets
unmapped:

  CPU0 deferred_split_scan()          CPU1 deferred_split_folio()
  list_del_init(&folio->_deferred_list)
    next->prev = prev
    prev->next = next
    entry->next = entry
                                      list_lru_lock_irqsave()
                                      folio_set_partially_mapped()
                                      __list_lru_add()
                                        list_empty(item)  -> true
                                        list_add_tail(item, &l->list)
                                          item->next = &l->list
                                          item->prev = tail
    entry->prev = entry

The folio now sits on the list_lru with ->prev pointing to itself. The
next removal leaves the neighbours pointing to it, and they still do so
after the folio has been freed. With CONFIG_DEBUG_LIST:

  list_del corruption. prev->next should be ffd4000000270090, but was
  ffd4000000278090. (prev=ffd4000000270090)

Fix it by grabbing the lock around list_del_init() so
deferred_split_folio() cannot race with it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/filemap: finish fault cleanup before dropping the fault lock

On a retried fault, a fatal signal interrupting the folio lock wait
makes lock_folio_maybe_drop_mmap() drop the fault lock without pinning
the file. However, filemap_fault() may still need to release
mapping->invalidate_lock. A concurrent munmap() can release the last
file reference and free the mapping before that unlock.

Defer dropping the fault lock to filemap_fault()'s retry cleanup, after
releasing invalidate_lock. If the fault lock was already dropped for
I/O, release the existing file reference instead. Keep the fault lock
held for FAULT_FLAG_RETRY_NOWAIT as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure

If ttm_bo_init_validate() fails, it drops the buffer object's reference
and cleans it up through the supplied destroy callback. lsdc_bo_destroy()
releases the GEM object and frees the enclosing lsdc_bo, so freeing it
again in lsdc_bo_create() causes a double free on a synchronous failure
path.

Let TTM own the cleanup after initialization has started and return the
error directly. Keep the explicit free on drm_gem_object_init() failure,
which occurs before ownership is passed to TTM.

Tested on LS7A2000 by making drm_vma_offset_add() return -ENOSPC for one
selected dumb-buffer creation. The error reached userspace, the destroy
callback ran once, and no handle was published or tracked BO retained.
Normal buffer creation, zeroing, mapping, readback and release passed.

AI assistance was used for the ownership analysis, fix, fault-injection
tools, build and test execution.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT

batadv_mesh_free() releases the translation tables via batadv_tt_free()
before batadv_originator_free() stops orig_work. The purge worker can
therefore still run while the TT is torn down. When an originator times
out, batadv_purge_orig_ref() calls batadv_tt_global_del_orig(), which
loads tt.global_hash and walks all buckets while taking their locks:

  CPU0                          CPU1
  batadv_tt_free()              batadv_purge_orig()
                                  batadv_tt_global_del_orig()
                                    hash = ...tt.global_hash;
    batadv_tt_global_table_free()
      batadv_hash_destroy(hash);
                                    spin_lock_bh(&hash->list_locks[i]);

Disable orig_work at the beginning of batadv_mesh_free(), directly after
the mesh was marked as deactivating. The second
disable_delayed_work_sync() in batadv_originator_free() is harmless because
it is free'd anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind

In [1], sashiko reported the following issue:

=== snip ===
Looking at how these fences are managed, drm_crtc_create_fence()
creates a dma_fence without taking a reference to the drm_device or
drm_crtc. Because the sync_file framework exposes this fence to
userspace, the fence can outlive the CRTC.

The dma_fence contract requires that data accessed by dma_fence_ops
(like get_driver_name) must remain valid for an RCU grace period after
the fence is signaled. However, drm_crtc_cleanup() and the subsequent
freeing of the device do not wait for an RCU grace period via
synchronize_rcu().

If userspace calls ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO) concurrently with a device
hot-unplug:

CPU1 (Userspace)
sync_file_get_name()
  ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops);
  if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag())
    // Preempted or delayed here

CPU2 (Driver Teardown)
Signals the fence (setting fence->ops = NULL)
Destroys and frees the CRTC without waiting for an RCU grace period

CPU1 (Resumes)
  ops->get_driver_name(fence) -> drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name()
  crtc = fence_to_crtc(fence); // Casts to the freed CRTC
  return crtc->dev->driver->name; // Use-after-free

...

Does the CRTC or DRM device need to be kept alive for the RCU grace
period, or should the fence hold a proper reference to prevent the
use-after-free when get_driver_name() and get_timeline_name() access
the freed CRTC structure?
=== snap ===

I believe this to be a correct observation and this patch implements
the suggestion of waiting for an RCU grace period before proceeding
with destruction of the drm_crtc, so that get_driver_name() and
get_timeline_name() can still work.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe

p9_virtio_probe() reads a 16-bit mount tag length (tag_len) from the
device config and kzalloc()s tag_len + 1 bytes for chan->tag with no
upper bound. A malicious or compromised host can present a tag of up to
65535 bytes; that tag is later copied into the single-page sysfs buffer
by p9_mount_tag_show() (memcpy(buf, chan->tag, tag_len + 1)), a
host-controlled out-of-bounds write of up to ~64 KiB past the PAGE_SIZE
attribute buffer.

Reject an overlong tag at probe time. A 9p mount tag is a name-like
identifier, so bound it by NAME_MAX (255): that limit is independent of
the sysfs/seq_file page size and is far above any legitimate mount tag,
which keeps p9_mount_tag_show() safe at the root without hard-coding a
seq_file implementation detail.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work

An IOPOLL ring without DEFER_TASKRUN can be reaped by a task other than
the one that submitted the I/O. If a polled request is marked
REQ_F_REISSUE, io_free_batch_list() calls io_queue_iowq() with the
original tctx. Ordinary task exit can tear down tctx->io_wq after
draining only the tracked requests. The live request pins the task, but
not its io-wq, so the foreign task can race io_wq_put_and_exit() and
enqueue through a freed or NULL queue.

Forward foreign userspace enqueues to the owning task before accessing
tctx->io_wq. Use a dedicated task_work callback so reissues still go
straight to io-wq, and fail them if task_work is running in cancellation
mode. Preserve the existing PF_KTHREAD cancellation path. This also
covers the other callers of io_queue_iowq() without changing the
worker-owned enqueue path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: free the task context after a grace period

A task other than the owner can free a request, io_ring_exit_work()
running the local task_work of a DEFER_TASKRUN ring for example, or
io_do_iopoll() reaping completions. io_put_task() then takes the else
branch:

    percpu_counter_sub(&tctx->inflight, 1);
    if (unlikely(atomic_read(&tctx->in_cancel)))
            wake_up(&tctx->wait);
    put_task_struct(tctx->task);

The first line is what lets the owner leave io_uring_cancel_generic(),
and on exec it frees the tctx right after. Nothing holds that off for
the remaining three lines, the task reference only covers a tctx freed
along with the task_struct. It used to work out because
io_uring_del_tctx_node() took the uring_lock that the freeing side holds
across io_put_task(), until that moved to tctx_lock.

Free the tctx with kfree_rcu(), and enter an RCU read section in
io_put_task() before the count is dropped.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference

io_wq_cancel_tw_create() inspects cb->func after calling
io_worker_cancel_cb(). For an existing worker, that call can drop the
last worker reference and wake io_worker_exit(). If the canceling task
is preempted, the worker can be unlinked and freed by kfree_rcu() before
the callback function is inspected. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free
read in this path.

Save whether the callback belongs to an unpublished continuation worker
while its reference is still held, then use the saved result for the
conditional free. This preserves the existing accounting and frees only
the worker allocated for the canceled continuation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes

A received TT change (OGM diff or full table response) with the ROAM flag
but without DEL is handled by batadv_tt_global_add() like a ROAMING_ADV:

* a newly created global entry gets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM and is
  therefore excluded from the global CRC. The sender has it in its local
  CRC and the receiver has to request the full table again
* batadv_tt_global_purge_local() removes the local entry of the
  receiver. The receiver's own client is considered as roamed to the sender
  and frames for it are rerouted

The ROAM flag only has a meaning together with DEL. Drop it on reception to
keep it from populating the global table with a temporary ROAMING entry
which is not part of the CRC - and therefore causing a CRC mismatch.

SportEase is a web application for managing school sports events, class rosters, and competition teams. Prior to 1.3, an authenticated account with is_profile_complete=false can submit an attacker-selected class_id for any class in the currently active event to PUT /api/user/profile during first profile completion. AuthHandler.UpdateProfile accepts the class without validating the user's legitimate membership and automatically derives and assigns the corresponding {class_name}_rep role while isFirstCompletion is true. The attacker can become representative of one selected class, view roster information including email addresses, and add or remove competition-team assignments. Downstream handlers correctly reject access to other classes, so the impact is bounded to the selected class, but the representative privilege cannot be revoked through the exposed API and requires direct database intervention or another out-of-band remediation method. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.

Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop') vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Excessive Allocation.

The Alt-Svc response header parser in src/hackney_altsvc.erl does not guarantee forward progress. When parse_token/2 receives a non-token, non-whitespace, non-comma byte (e.g. !, @, =, ;), it returns the input unchanged. skip_comma/1 also returns the buffer unchanged when the first byte is not a comma. parse_entries/2 then recurses with identical data, creating a tight infinite tail-recursive loop that pins a scheduler at 100% CPU. The calling process never returns.

The entry point parse_and_cache/3 is called synchronously in the connection process on every HTTP response. A single-byte Alt-Svc: ! response header is sufficient to trigger the hang; the header is fully controlled by any HTTP origin the client connects to.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.0.1.

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Flooding.

The URL parser in src/hackney_url.erl converts every unrecognized URL scheme to a permanent BEAM atom via binary_to_atom/2. BEAM atoms are never garbage-collected and the atom table defaults to a hard limit of 1,048,576 entries. An attacker who can supply URLs with attacker-chosen scheme prefixes — directly as request targets, as configured webhook URLs, or via Location headers followed during redirects — can exhaust the atom table and crash the entire BEAM VM with system_limit.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0 before 4.0.1.

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Flooding.

The SOCKS5 transport in src/hackney_socks5.erl correctly applies the caller-supplied timeout to the SOCKS5 negotiation phase, but then upgrades the connection to TLS using the two-argument form ssl:connect/2, which defaults to an infinite timeout. The Timeout value is in scope at the call site but is not forwarded. A hostile SOCKS5 proxy that completes the SOCKS5 handshake normally and then goes silent (or sends a partial TLS ServerHello and stalls) will cause the connecting process to block indefinitely, regardless of the connect_timeout or recv_timeout options supplied by the caller.

This issue affects hackney: from 0.8.1 before 4.0.1.

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection') vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows HTTP Request/Response Splitting.

The WebSocket upgrade code in src/hackney_ws.erl copies the host, path, headers (ExtraHeaders), and protocols options from the caller-supplied opts map into the internal #ws_data{} record in init/1 and then splices them verbatim into the raw HTTP/1.1 upgrade request by binary concatenation in do_handshake/1. No CRLF or NUL stripping is performed at any of these four injection sites. An attacker who controls any of these options — for example by forwarding URL components or header values from untrusted input into hackney_ws:start_link/1 — can inject arbitrary HTTP headers into the outbound WebSocket upgrade request, leading to header injection, credential spoofing toward the upstream server, log and cache poisoning, or request smuggling via intermediary proxies.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.0.1.

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Flooding.

The WebSocket client in src/hackney_ws.erl imposes no upper bound on memory consumption in three code paths. First, read_handshake_response/3 accumulates received bytes into a growing buffer with no size cap; the per-receive timeout resets on every chunk, so a server that streams bytes without ever sending \r\n\r\n causes the buffer to grow until memory is exhausted. Second, parse_payload/9 and parse_active_payload/8 do not validate the declared frame payload length against any limit; because RFC 6455 allows payload lengths up to 2^63-1 bytes, a server that announces a very large frame and dribbles bytes causes the accumulation buffer to grow until OOM. Third, the frag_buffer field in #ws_data{} accumulates continuation frames indefinitely; a server that sends an endless stream of non-final (nofin) fragmented frames without ever sending a final (fin) frame grows frag_buffer without bound.

In all three cases the attacker only needs to control the WebSocket server the hackney client connects to, with no authentication or special client configuration required.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.0.1.

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows HTTP Request Splitting.

hackney does not percent-encode carriage return (\r) or line feed (\n) characters in the URL query component before constructing the HTTP/1.1 request target. Characters outside the grammar defined in RFC 3986 Section 3.4 must be percent-encoded, but hackney_url:make_url/3 passes the query binary directly without validation or escaping. An attacker who can control all or part of a URL passed to hackney can inject raw CRLF sequences into the query string, which are then sent as HTTP line breaks in the request target. This enables injection of arbitrary HTTP headers or splitting of the HTTP request.

This issue affects hackney: from 0.1.0 before 4.0.1.

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Flooding.

hackney_h3:await_response_loop/6 accumulates the HTTP/3 response body in memory without any size cap. The after Timeout clause is a per-message inactivity timer that resets on every received chunk, housekeeping message, or settings frame — it is not a wall-clock deadline. A malicious HTTP/3 server that emits one small chunk every Timeout - 1 ms with Fin = false and never sends a final frame keeps the loop alive indefinitely while the accumulation buffer grows linearly without bound, eventually exhausting the BEAM process heap and causing an out-of-memory condition.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.0.1.

Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in ninenines gun (gun_http module) allows a malicious server to exhaust client memory via unbounded HTTP/1.1 response buffering.

In gun_http:handle/5, three clauses accumulate incoming TCP data into the connection's buffer field using binary concatenation with no upper-bound check: the head clause appends data until the \r\n\r\n header terminator is found; the body_chunked clause appends data whenever cow_http_te:stream_chunked/2 returns a more result indicating an incomplete chunk boundary; and the body_trailer clause appends data until the trailing \r\n\r\n is found. In each case, when the expected terminator never arrives, the enlarged binary is stored back into state and the process waits for more data, with no configurable or hard-coded ceiling on buffer size.

A malicious or compromised server can exploit this by sending a partial response that never completes. For example, a response may begin with HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-Pad:  followed by an unbounded stream of arbitrary bytes, never sending the header terminator. The gun connection process will continuously append the incoming data to its buffer, causing unbounded heap growth. Because BEAM imposes no per-process heap limit by default, a single malicious connection can exhaust all available memory on the node, causing a node-wide out-of-memory crash.

This issue affects gun: from 1.0.0-pre.1 before 2.4.0.

Unexpected Status Code or Return Value vulnerability in ninenines gun (gun_http module) allows a malicious HTTP server to force the client into raw protocol mode via an unsolicited 101 Switching Protocols response.

In gun_http:handle_inform/8, when a 101 Switching Protocols response is received over HTTP/1.1, the function verifies only that the Upgrade header is syntactically valid and that the stream reference is a plain reference(). It does not check whether the client ever sent an Upgrade or Connection: upgrade header on the corresponding request. Because this check is absent, any 101 response (solicited or not) causes gun to dispatch a gun_upgrade message to the caller and transition the entire connection to raw protocol mode.

A malicious or compromised HTTP server can send an unsolicited 101 response to any HTTP/1.1 request, causing the gun client to abandon HTTP framing for that connection. Once in raw mode, gun_raw applies no flow control (flow=infinity) and re-arms socket active mode after every received packet, so the server can flood the client with arbitrary bytes. These are forwarded as unbounded gun_data messages to the owner process, exhausting its mailbox and BEAM memory, ultimately crashing the VM.

This issue affects gun: from 2.0.0-pre.1 before 2.4.0.

Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) vulnerability in wojtekmach Req allows attacker-controlled HTTP servers to exhaust memory in a Req client via decompression-bomb response bodies.

Req's default response pipeline includes Req.Steps.decode_body/1 and Req.Steps.decompress_body/1 in lib/req/steps.ex. decode_body/1 dispatches on the server-supplied content-type (or URL extension) and calls :zip.extract(body, [:memory]) for application/zip, :erl_tar.extract({:binary, body}, [:memory]) for application/x-tar, and :erl_tar.extract({:binary, body}, [:memory, :compressed]) for application/gzip / .tgz. Each returns the full decompressed archive contents as a [{name, bytes}] list in memory, with no per-entry or total size cap. decompress_body/1 walks the content-encoding header and chains :zlib/:brotli/:ezstd decoders, so a response advertising content-encoding: gzip, gzip, gzip inflates through multiple layers without bound.

Both steps are enabled by default, no caller opt-in is required, and the attacker controls the content-type and content-encoding headers on their own server (or on any host reached via Req's automatic redirect following). A sub-megabyte response can expand to multiple gigabytes on the victim, crashing the BEAM process.

This issue affects req: from 0.1.0 before 0.6.1.

The Erlang/OTP ssl application does not validate that the PSK identity list and binder list carried in a TLS 1.3 ClientHello pre-shared key extension have equal length before passing them to the session ticket handler. In tls_handshake_1_3:handle_pre_shared_key/3, an OfferedPreSharedKeys record with a mismatched number of identities and binders is forwarded directly to tls_server_session_ticket:use/4, which crashes the session ticket handler process.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a single crafted ClientHello to a TLS 1.3 server with session tickets enabled (stateful or stateless mode) and permanently disrupt session ticket handling on that listener. New TLS 1.3 handshakes complete but subsequently crash when the server attempts to issue a session ticket, effectively making TLS 1.3 unusable on the affected listener until the ssl application is restarted. TLS 1.2 connections are not affected.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 22.2 before OTP 27.3.4.14, OTP 28.5.0.3, and OTP 29.0.3, corresponding to ssl from 9.5 before 11.2.12.10, 11.6.0.3, and 11.7.3.

Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions vulnerability in Erlang OTP erts (epmd) allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to permanently terminate the Erlang Port Mapper Daemon (epmd) via connection slot exhaustion.

The do_accept function in erts/epmd/src/epmd_srv.c calls epmd_cleanup_exit() when accept(2) returns EMFILE (per-process file descriptor limit reached) or ENFILE (system-wide file descriptor limit reached), rather than treating these as recoverable conditions. An attacker can exhaust epmd's file descriptor slots by holding many TCP connections open while periodically sending a single byte to reset the idle timeout, then causing accept(2) to return EMFILE, which kills the daemon. epmd has no per-source-IP connection cap, making the attack feasible from a single source.

On Debian/Ubuntu default packaging the impact is amplified: the systemd unit inherits a low file descriptor soft limit, and repeated daemon deaths trigger systemd's start-rate-limit, permanently failing both epmd.service and epmd.socket and requiring manual operator intervention to recover.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.15, OTP 28.5.0.4, and OTP 29.0.4, corresponding to erts from 6.0 before 15.2.7.11, 16.4.0.4, and 17.0.4.

Integer Underflow (Wrap or Wraparound) vulnerability in erlang otp erlang/otp (erts modules), erlang otp erts (erts modules) allows Forced Integer Overflow, Excessive Allocation. This vulnerability is associated with program files erts/emulator/beam/external.c, emulator/beam/external.c.

The BIT_BINARY_EXT tag (77) handler in the External Term Format (ETF) decoder accepts an encoding with both length and trailing-bits fields set to zero. The subsequent computation of the bitstring size underflows an unsigned integer, producing a value of roughly 2^64 that is then passed as a memory allocation size. The allocator aborts the entire node with a message such as Cannot allocate 2305843009213693951 bytes of memory (of type "binary").

The crash is a VM-level abort, not an Erlang-level exception. It cannot be intercepted by supervision trees, by try/catch, or by passing the [safe] option to binary_to_term/2 (which only restricts atom creation and does not perform structural validation of binary encodings).

Any application that decodes ETF from untrusted sources via binary_to_term/1,2 or enif_binary_to_term() is exposed. The Erlang distribution protocol also decodes incoming terms through the same code path, but distribution is expected to run on trusted networks per the OTP Secure Coding Guidelines (DSG-011).

This issue affects OTP from OTP 27.0 before OTP 27.3.4.15, OTP 28.5.0.4, and OTP 29.0.4, corresponding to erts from 15.0 before 15.2.7.11, 16.4.0.4, and 17.0.4.

Signed to Unsigned Conversion Error and Out-of-bounds Write vulnerability in Erlang OTP erts allows an attacker who can supply a crafted Erlang external term format (ETF) binary to binary_to_term/1 to corrupt the BEAM heap pointer and crash the virtual machine.

When decoding a LARGE_TUPLE_EXT term, the validation pass decoded_size() in erts/emulator/beam/external.c reads the 32-bit arity field as unsigned (get_uint32()), while the decode pass dec_term() reads the same field as a signed 32-bit integer (get_int32()) into an int. An arity wire value of 0x80000000 passes validation as 2147483648 but decodes as -2147483648, so the subsequent hp += n moves the heap allocation pointer backward. Neither pass enforces the runtime tuple-arity limit MAX_ARITYVAL. The result is an out-of-bounds heap write; in practice the VM detects an impossible heap size and aborts, denying service. The required padding is large when uncompressed but the compressed-ETF envelope shrinks it to a small payload on the wire.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 25.0 before OTP 27.3.4.15, OTP 28.5.0.4, and OTP 29.0.4, corresponding to erts from 13.0 before 15.2.7.11, 16.4.0.4, and 17.0.4.

The Erlang/OTP ssl application does not detect cycles when reconstructing an incomplete peer certificate chain during a TLS or DTLS handshake. In ssl_certificate:handle_incomplete_chain/5, the received chain is passed to ssl_certificate:build_certificate_chain/5, which walks issuer relationships via ssl_certificate:do_certificate_chain/7 with no cycle detection and no depth limit. When the peer supplies two mutually cross-signed certificates in unordered form (A issues B, B issues A), the issuer lookup alternates between the two certificates and the pair of functions recurses indefinitely, growing the call stack and chain accumulator without bound.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted certificate chain in a TLS or DTLS Certificate handshake message to exhaust available memory and crash the BEAM node. Only a TCP connection and a partial handshake are required; no authentication or completed handshake is needed, and both TLS/DTLS servers and clients are affected when processing peer certificate messages.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 23.2 before OTP 27.3.4.15, OTP 28.5.0.4, and OTP 29.0.4, corresponding to ssl from 10.2 before 11.2.12.11, 11.6.0.4, and 11.7.4.

Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity vulnerability in the traversal engine in rrrene html_sanitize_ex allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust server CPU and memory via a flat run of sibling elements in sanitized HTML. The list clause of HtmlSanitizeEx.Traverser.traverse/2 recurses on the tail of a sibling list and then evaluates List.flatten([head] ++ tail) over the already flattened result, so every one of n siblings copies and re-walks the entire remaining tail. The flattening is only needed for the rare case where scrub returns several replacement nodes for one node, but the cost is paid across the whole tail at every step, making traversal quadratic in sibling count.

The traverser sits on every public entry point, so no particular scrubber or configuration is required and the payload needs only allowed tags. A 160 KB body of 20,000 sibling elements occupies a scheduler for roughly 1.7 seconds, and the cost grows faster than the body does.

This issue affects html_sanitize_ex: from 0.3.1 before 1.4.5 and from 1.5.0-rc.0 before 1.5.3.

A flaw was found in RESTEasy's SourceProvider. This vulnerability allows an unauthenticated attacker to perform an unauthenticated remote file read. By sending a specially crafted XML body with a DOCTYPE declaration referencing external entities to an endpoint that accepts application/xml and returns Source or StreamSource, the server can be tricked into resolving the entity and including sensitive file contents in the HTTP response. This is due to the SourceProvider.writeTo() method creating a SAXParser without disabling external entity resolution, leading to an XML External Entity (XXE) vulnerability.

A flaw was found in Netty RtspDecoder. The `RtspMethods.valueOf()` function incorrectly strips trailing control bytes from method tokens in Real-Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) requests. A remote attacker can exploit this by sending a specially crafted RTSP request, leading to method-token smuggling. This vulnerability allows an attacker to bypass method-based access controls and can also be used to launder malicious requests through Netty-based RTSP proxies, making them appear legitimate to backend systems.

A denial-of-service flaw was found in gnome-remote-desktop. An unauthenticated remote attacker can open RDP connections without completing the handshake and retain the connection-throttling slots indefinitely because no pre-authentication handshake deadline is enforced. By exhausting the global connection limit, an attacker can prevent new RDP clients from connecting until a holding socket is closed.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition product of Oracle Analytics (component: Analytics Server).  Supported versions that are affected are 8.2.0.0.0 and  26.01.0.0.0. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.5 (Confidentiality impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).
Double free in Windows Image Acquisition allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.
Insufficient granularity of access control in Windows IKE Extension allows an authorized attacker to perform spoofing locally.
Improper link resolution before file access ('link following') in Windows iSCSI allows an unauthorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.
Time-of-check time-of-use (toctou) race condition in Windows DHCP Server allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network.

A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 stream teardown can leak response memory, including the contents of other connections' response buffers, to a peer. When a stream is torn down while a write is still backpressured, for example by a peer `RST_STREAM` or by the server's own per-stream timeout destroying the stream, the stream's response buffer is freed but a reference to it is still used, so freed or unrelated heap memory is written to the socket instead of the intended response. On Node.js 26.x and 24.x the teardown can be driven purely by a remote peer once the window-size change from 26.9.0 and 24.22.0 is present, and on all supported lines the same defect is reachable through an application-initiated teardown such as a per-stream idle timeout. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

Apache WSS4J remembers the UsernameToken Nonce, the Timestamp and signature of a signed message, and the ID of a SAML 2.0 "OneTimeUse" assertion, so that a captured message cannot be accepted twice. It checked whether a value had already been seen, validated the message, and only then remembered the value, as two separate steps. If several copies of the same message were processed at the same time, they could all pass the check before any of them was remembered, and all be accepted. An attacker who obtained a valid message before the recipient first processed it could send several copies at once, so that the same authenticated request was executed more than once. Where a UsernameToken is not bound to the message by a signature, the copies could carry different message bodies. The attacker needs to obtain the message while it is still in transit; a message captured after it has been accepted cannot be replayed. Affects deployments with a replay cache configured, as Apache CXF has by default. The value is now checked and remembered in a single atomic step. Custom ReplayCache implementations should override the new ReplayCache.addIfAbsent method with an operation that is atomic in their underlying store. Users are recommended to upgrade to versions 4.0.3 or 3.0.7 or 2.4.5, which fix this issue.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED ** Missing authentication for critical function vulnerability in Apache Griffin Web Service. The REST API does not have any authentication. This includes sensitive endpoints, such as job submission when a Livy/Spark backend is configured. The API must be properly secured on the network level, and this fact was arguably not documented as clearly as it could have.



This issue affects Apache Griffin Web Service: all versions.



As this project is retired, we do not plan to release a version that fixes this issue. Users are recommended to find an alternative or restrict access to the instance to trusted users.



NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Installation and Configuration).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.5 (Confidentiality impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Reconciliation Manage).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Hyperion Financial Close Management accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.5 (Confidentiality impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N).

In the Apache Airflow Microsoft Azure provider 10.2.0 through 15.3.0, `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` turned off TLS certificate verification for its connection to Amazon S3 by default (`s3_verify=False`), whatever the AWS connection's own verification settings were. An attacker positioned on the network between an Airflow worker and S3 could intercept that traffic, read the signed requests and alter the listed object keys and the copied file contents. Deployments are affected when a Dag uses `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` without setting `s3_verify`. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-microsoft-azure 15.3.1 or later, which uses the AWS connection's verification settings by default.

Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File vulnerability in the Apache Iggy server. If Apache Iggy 0.9.0 started without IGGY_ROOT_USERNAME and IGGY_ROOT_PASSWORD, it generated a root password and wrote it to the server log file, which is enabled by default. The system snapshot command (GetSnapshot on the binary transports and POST /snapshot on HTTP) let a user with only the read_servers permission download the server log files. That user could read the generated root password and log in as root.

This issue affects Apache Iggy: 0.9.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.10.0, which fixes the issue. Version 0.10.0 never generates a root password, and the snapshot requires the manage_servers permission. If a 0.9.0 server generated its root password, change that password.

Grav from 2.0.0 before 2.2.18 contains a resource exhaustion vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to fill the disk by varying the HTTP Host header. Attackers can send requests with distinct Host values to create per-host compiled configuration, blueprint, language and page index caches, causing session, upload and logging failures.

Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL
pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA
records.

Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial
of Service).

CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference

Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at
least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2)
usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted
CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of
associated TLSA records.

DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the
DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable
in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim
MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.

Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also
unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.

Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI
are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses
OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.

FIPS impact: no
The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

PHPGurukul Employee Leaves Management System V2.1 contains an information disclosure vulnerability because database backup files are stored within the publicly accessible web root. An unauthenticated remote attacker can download the SQL backup files and retrieve sensitive database contents, including employee personally identifiable information and password hashes.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reclaim credits for decrypted reads with no matching mid

When a decrypted SMB2 READ response carries a MessageId that matches no
outstanding request, both the inline receive_encrypted_read() and the
offloaded smb2_decrypt_offload() paths drop the frame without accounting
the credits the server granted in it.  The plaintext unknown-frame path in
cifs_demultiplex_thread() already reclaims them with
smb2_add_credits_from_hdr(), so encrypted reads leak credits that the
plaintext path would not.

This also happens for legitimate frames - e.g. a reply that arrives after
the client has timed out and dropped the mid - so over a long-lived
connection the client's credit count drifts down and can eventually starve
it of the ability to issue requests.  The frame is AEAD-authenticated, so
the granted credits in the decrypted header come from the real server and
are safe to apply.

Reclaim the credits from the decrypted header before dropping the frame,
and export smb2_add_credits_from_hdr() so the SMB2 receive paths can use it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: don't resurrect an exiting tcon from cached dir workers

cfids_laundromat_worker() bumps tcon->tc_count for every expired open
cfid and queues cached_dir_offload_close() without checking whether the
tcon is already being torn down.  Racing with the final cifs_put_tcon(),
the tcon comes back from zero and gets torn down twice:

  T1                                  T2
  cifs_put_tcon()
   --tc_count == 0, TID_EXITING
   tconInfoFree()
    free_cached_dirs()
     cancel_delayed_work_sync()       cfids_laundromat_worker()
                                       ++tc_count == 1
                                       queue_work(serverclose_wq)
    kfree(tcon->origin_fullpath)
    kfree(tcon)
                                      cached_dir_offload_close()
                                       close_cached_dir()  [UAF]
                                       cifs_put_tcon()
                                        tconInfoFree()     [double free]

cached_dir_lease_break() also bumps tc_count without tc_lock, racing with
the laundromat's locked update.

Take the tcon reference through a helper that refuses once the tcon is
TID_EXITING or its refcount has dropped to zero.  Queued put_work and
close_work then always hold a tcon reference, so tconInfoFree() can't
run before they finish and free_cached_dirs() doesn't need to flush any
workqueue.  If the laundromat can't get a reference, put the cfid back on
the dying list for free_cached_dirs() to free; its handle goes away with
the tree connection.

The lease break path finds the tcon on ses->tcon_list under
cifs_tcp_ses_lock, so it can't see TID_EXITING, but it now takes tc_lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: server: size directory name conversion buffer correctly

A 2048-byte ASCII directory name needs 4098 bytes when converted to
UTF-16, including the terminator. ksmbd_convert_dir_info_name() caps
its allocation at PATH_MAX and writes past the end of that buffer.

Allocate space for one UTF-16 code unit per input byte plus the
terminator. Use kmalloc_array() to check the size calculation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mt76: mt7996: unlink TWT flow if the MCU rejects the agreement

mt7996_mac_add_twt_setup() links a new flow into dev->twt_list before
asking the MCU to add the agreement, but exits without unlinking the flow
if the request fails. The flow-ID and table masks are only committed
after MCU success, so the still-linked flow is invisible to the
mask-gated teardown paths.

If the station retries the setup, the same slot is cleared and its
embedded list node reinitialized while it is still linked, corrupting
dev->twt_list. If the station disassociates instead, teardown skips the
flow and station storage can be freed while the node remains linked. A
later scheduling or debugfs twt_stats walk can then dereference the
freed flow, resulting in a use-after-free.

Unlink the flow when the MCU rejects the agreement. This restores the
list to its pre-request state while leaving the unchanged mask and
agreement accounting untouched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: do not pass a NULL buf to is_oplock_break()

receive_encrypted_read() sets *num_mids = 1 and never writes the
caller's bufs[]. Offload returns -1 with *num_mids = 0, so the
demultiplex thread skips the frame. The inline decrypt path
returns 0 even when smb2_find_mid() fails.

cifs_demultiplex_thread() then treats mids[i] == NULL as an
oplock break and calls is_oplock_break(bufs[i], server) with
bufs[i] still NULL. smb2_is_valid_oplock_break() reads
hdr.Command at offset 12 and oopses.

A large encrypted READ whose MessageId does not match is enough
to panic cifsd.

    Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address
    0xdffffc0000000001: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
    KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range
    [0x0000000000000008-0x000000000000000f]
    CPU: 0 PID: 100 Comm: cifsd
    RIP: smb2_is_valid_oplock_break+0xc8/0x2270 [cifs]
    cifs_demultiplex_thread
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: release failed pending sockets of a listener

A child of a listener only left the listen.pending or listen.ready
list via smbdirect_socket_accept() or when the listener was
destroyed. So every connection that failed before it was accepted
(negotiate timeout, peer disconnect, invalid negotiate request, ...)
stayed on the list and counted against the backlog until the listener
was destroyed. After about backlog (10 for ksmbd) such connections
smbdirect_listen_connect_request() rejected every new connection with
-EBUSY, so an unauthenticated peer was able to permanently stop
ksmbd from accepting SMB-Direct connections.

Now a failed child moves itself to a new listen.orphaned list at the
end of smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work(), after the disconnect was
started, and queues listen.purge_orphaned_work, which releases it
with smbdirect_socket_release(), without holding the listener's
rdma_lock_handler() lock, in the same way smbdirect_socket_destroy()
does for the remaining children. Orphaned sockets still count against
the backlog until they are released.

sc->accept.listener is now only changed under listener->listen.lock
and whoever clears it is responsible for releasing the socket:
smbdirect_socket_accept(), purge_orphaned_work or the destroy of the
listener.

In order to make that work:

- a struct smbdirect_socket that is a listener is now freed via
  kfree_rcu(), so that a child can dereference sc->accept.listener
  under rcu_read_lock(), even if the listener is released concurrently.

- smbdirect_listen_connect_request() adds nsc to the listen.pending
  list and sets nsc->accept.listener before it calls
  smbdirect_accept_connect_request(), and always returns 0 so the
  rdma_cm core keeps the connection id and nsc owns it. On a non-zero
  return it schedules nsc's teardown with
  smbdirect_socket_schedule_cleanup(), which orphans it off the
  listener so that purge_orphaned_work releases it; nsc destroys its
  own connection id with rdma_destroy_id() in that teardown. The
  teardown has to be deferred because the rdma_cm core holds nsc's
  id_priv->handler_mutex across the handler, so nsc->rdma.cm_id must
  not be destroyed synchronously from here. That same handler_mutex
  (and the listener's) also guarantees nsc can't go away under us,
  so setting the listener before the call is safe and lets a failure
  orphan nsc.

- smbdirect_accept_negotiate_recv_work() no longer moves a socket to
  the ready list if it already failed or no longer belongs to the
  listener. Every accepting socket has a listener, so if
  sc->accept.listener is already cleared, it no longer sends a
  negotiate response, as the socket is about to be released.

- smbdirect_socket_destroy() of the listener disables
  purge_orphaned_work and also releases the orphaned sockets.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: don't wait for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync()

smbdirect_socket_destroy_sync() waited for RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED
after smbdirect_socket_cleanup_work() called rdma_disconnect(). That
can take very long, e.g. if the peer just disappeared, until the
rdma cm gives up, or forever if the event already happened, but the
status was overwritten afterwards.

This is not needed: smbdirect_socket_destroy() drains the qp under
rdma_lock_handler(), destroys it and calls rdma_destroy_id(), which
only waits for a currently running event handler and makes sure no
further events are delivered. The rest of the disconnect protocol
(DREQ/DREP and timewait for IB, abrupt close for iWarp) is handled
by the rdma core asynchronously. drivers/nvme/host/rdma.c also just
calls rdma_disconnect() and ib_drain_qp() before rdma_destroy_id().

So smbdirect_socket_destroy() now also accepts
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTING and changes the status to
SMBDIRECT_SOCKET_DISCONNECTED itself under rdma_lock_handler().

We could still get RDMA_CM_EVENT_DISCONNECTED in the small
windows between rdma_unlock_handler() and rdma_destroy_id(),
but in that case smbdirect_connection_rdma_event_handler()
is basically a no-op.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.6 to 3.10.3, XMLCorpusView._read_xml_fragment accumulates 1 KiB blocks and repeatedly applies whole-buffer XML validation while a comment or CDATA terminator remains ahead. A large comment in an attacker-controlled corpus file causes quadratic CPU consumption through documented XML corpus readers across the affected range. On 3.6 and 3.9.2, a large CDATA section incurs the quadratic scan before rejection, while on 3.10.3 both comment and CDATA documents are read successfully. This vulnerability is fixed in 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. Prior to 3.10.4, WordNet Synset.tree and acyclic_tree traverse relation graphs through recursive utility helpers without a depth bound. Exploitation requires the host application to load an attacker-influenced custom or foreign WordNet-format lexical resource; no relation in NLTK's bundled WordNet 3.0 corpus reaches the crash threshold. An excessively deep relation graph in such a resource can exceed the Python recursion limit and terminate the traversal or request worker. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) is a suite of open source Python modules, data sets, and tutorials supporting research and development in Natural Language Processing. From 3.10.0 until 3.10.4, TokenSearcher.findall and Text.findall accept caller-controlled regular expressions with an unbounded number of capturing groups throughout the affected range. Starting in 3.10.3, nltk.redos.compile and RegexpTokenizer expose the same compile-time vector. The third-party regex engine compiles group-dense patterns with roughly quadratic cost before the match-time timeout begins, allowing a small unauthenticated request to exhaust CPU and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 3.10.4.

Go-Guerrilla SMTP Daemon is a lightweight SMTP server written in Go. In 1.6.7 and earlier, according to the repository advisory's structured affected range, server.go defines the seven-byte cmdXCLIENT token, but the XCLIENT handler slices input[8:] after matching only that seven-byte verb, so a bare command causes an out-of-bounds panic in handleClient and terminates the daemon because that connection goroutine does not recover the panic. The issue is reachable by an unauthenticated client when the non-default xclient_on setting is enabled; no HELO command is required. The repository fix is present in version 1.6.7-1.

aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.12.1, the QoS 2 transaction handler in amqtt/mqtt/protocol/handler.py, _handle_qos2_message_flow(), can retain transaction state and packet identifiers when a client disconnects before the handshake completes, unlike QoS 1 flows that expire after the default five-second timeout. A remote client can repeatedly begin QoS 2 flows and disconnect without maintaining long-lived connections; anonymous clients can do this with the default configuration, while authenticated deployments remain affected when a client may initiate QoS 2 flows. The retained state grows broker memory until resource exhaustion can terminate the process; no confidentiality or integrity impact is identified. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.1.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could access RapidDiag process metadata and log file inventory information through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because certain RapidDiag REST API endpoints accept a factory-default shared key for node authentication, which lets requests bypass Splunk user authentication.
For more information see Using RapidDiag (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/troubleshoot/9.0/contact-splunk-support/using-rapiddiag) and Secure Splunk Enterprise services with pass4SymmKey (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.0/secure-distributed-and-clustered-splunk-environments/secure-splunk-enterprise-services-with-pass4symmkey) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could access live event data from the indexing pipeline through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API on a standalone instance or a search head that is not an indexer cluster member.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise accepts an empty shared key during service authentication.
